intro: Email delivery rate is the share of sent emails that were actually accepted by the recipient's mail server, rather than bouncing. Enter emails sent and delivered to get the rate.

sections.heading: How Delivery Rate is calculated
sections.body: Delivery Rate = Delivered Emails ÷ Emails Sent — [the same delivered-over-sent shape most ESP reporting uses](https://www.mailtrap.io/blog/email-bounce-rate/), equivalent to (Sent − Bounced) ÷ Sent. Delivered here means the receiving mail server accepted the message; it says nothing about where that message ended up once it arrived.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: 9,800 ÷ 10,000 = 98.00%. This tells you 98% of sends were accepted somewhere by the recipient's mail server — it doesn't say how many of those 9,800 actually reached an inbox instead of a spam or promotions folder.

sections.heading: "Delivered" is not the same as "reached the inbox"
sections.body: [Delivery rate tells you whether your emails were received by the recipient's mail server; deliverability is a separate question about where the message lands once it's there](https://www.litmus.com/blog/the-difference-between-deliverability-and-delivery-rate) — the inbox, a spam folder, or a promotions tab. A campaign can post a 98% delivery rate while a meaningful share of those "delivered" messages never reach a primary inbox at all. High delivery rate and strong deliverability aren't the same accomplishment; delivery rate alone can't confirm the second one.

sections.heading: Delivery Rate vs. Bounce Rate
sections.body: These are near-complements built from the same sent count, but from opposite directions. Delivery Rate is delivered emails over sent — how much got through. [Bounce Rate](/calculators/bounce-rate-email) is bounced emails over sent — how much didn't. Delivery Rate plus Bounce Rate will land close to 100% for most sends, though not always exactly, since some sent emails can end up in neither bucket depending on how a specific ESP classifies deferred or in-progress sends at the moment a report is pulled.

faq.a: Email delivery rate is the percentage of sent emails that were successfully accepted by the recipient's mail server rather than bouncing, calculated as delivered emails divided by emails sent. It's the earliest checkpoint in email performance reporting — before open rate, click-to-open rate, or any engagement metric can be measured. A high delivery rate confirms the receiving server accepted the message; it doesn't confirm the message reached a primary inbox, since deliverability (where the message actually lands) is a separate, distinct question from delivery rate alone. A delivery rate close to 100% is typical for a clean, well-maintained list, while a noticeably lower rate usually points to list-hygiene problems worth investigating separately.

faq.q: How do you calculate Delivery Rate?
faq.a: Divide delivered emails by emails sent: Delivery Rate = Delivered ÷ Sent. A campaign that sent 10,000 emails with 9,800 delivered has a delivery rate of 9,800 ÷ 10,000 = 98.00%. Both figures need to describe the same send and the same reporting window — delivered counts from a broader time range than the sent count they're divided by will overstate the rate. Delivered can never legitimately exceed sent, since every delivered message was necessarily sent first; a result where it does signals a data or reporting mismatch, not a real delivery rate above 100%. Most email service providers calculate and surface this figure automatically in campaign reporting, so it rarely needs to be computed from raw send logs.

faq.q: Does a high delivery rate mean my emails reach the inbox?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Delivery rate only confirms the receiving mail server accepted the message rather than bouncing it — it says nothing about whether that message landed in the primary inbox, a spam folder, or a promotions tab. Deliverability, a related but distinct concept, is specifically about where an accepted message ends up. A sender can have a strong delivery rate and still have real deliverability problems if a large share of accepted messages are routing to spam. Delivery rate is a necessary first checkpoint, not proof the message was actually seen. Tools that specifically test inbox placement across major mailbox providers exist precisely because delivery rate alone can't answer that question.
